title: Quantum Chaos and Quantum Optimal Transport
abstract: Chaos in classical systems can be characterized by Lyapunov exponents that measure the exponential divergence of nearby trajectories, but directly extending this framework to quantum mechanics has been a persistent challenge. The wavelike nature of quantum states and the non-commutative geometry of quantum phase space obstruct a straightforward generalization of classical chaos theory. Here we develop a rigorous approach to quantum chaos by leveraging quantum optimal transport theory, which provides the missing geometric foundation for measuring distances between extended quantum distributions. We define quantum Lyapunov exponents that naturally avoid divergences encountered when naïvely generalizing classical exponents, and show that in the semiclassical limit they recover the classical global expansion rate, and hence the usual maximal Lyapunov exponent when they coincide. Our framework provides a tight connection between the divergence of classical trajectories and semiclassical phase space evolution, and additionally clarifies the role of out-of-time-order correlators as diagnostics of quantum chaos. These results establish quantum optimal transport as a unifying mathematical foundation for quantum chaos theory, providing new tools to characterize dynamical behavior across the full range of quantum dynamics from simple few-body models to complex many-body systems.
summary: This work develops a rigorous theory of quantum chaos by employing Quantum Optimal Transport (QOT) theory as a geometric foundation. It defines a quantum Lyapunov exponent that successfully avoids mathematical divergences inherent in naive generalizations. The key finding is that this quantum exponent recovers the classical maximal Lyapunov exponent in the semiclassical limit, establishing QOT as the unifying tool for the field.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of rigorously extending classical chaos theory, characterized by Lyapunov exponents, to the quantum domain due to the wavelike nature of quantum states and non-commutative phase space geometry.
main_result: Quantum Optimal Transport (QOT) theory provides a unifying mathematical foundation for quantum chaos, leading to a quantum Lyapunov exponent that recovers the classical maximal Lyapunov exponent in the semiclassical limit.
method: The authors define quantum Lyapunov exponents by leveraging the Wasserstein distance (a metric from QOT) applied to phase-space distributions (like the Husimi distribution) to measure the divergence of quantum states over time.
model_or_system: The framework is general, applicable to quantum systems ranging from simple few-body models to complex many-body systems, analyzed through the evolution of quantum states in phase space.
key_observables: Quantum Lyapunov exponents ($\lambda_q$), classical Lyapunov exponents ($\lambda_{cl}$), Out-of-Time-Order Correlators (OTOCs), and the Quantum Optimal Transport distance ($W_p$).
important_parameters: The semiclassical limit ($\hbar 	o 0$) is crucial for recovering classical results; the initial separation of states must be carefully chosen to avoid divergences.
main_assumptions: The approach relies on building upon modern noncommutative quantum optimal transport frameworks and defining admissible quantum distances satisfying specific axioms.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the comparison between classical trajectory divergence, quantum state evolution as extended distributions, and how QOT provides a natural distance metric respecting non-commutativity.
paper_structure: The paper develops the theory by first establishing the need for QOT, then defining the quantum Lyapunov exponent via the time evolution of the QOT distance, and finally proving its connection to the classical expansion rate and comparing it to OTOC diagnostics.
why_interesting: It provides a powerful, geometrically grounded tool (QOT) to quantify chaos in quantum systems, bridging the gap between classical dynamical systems theory and quantum dynamics, which is vital for understanding quantum thermalization and scrambling.
